To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) utility regulators must act ratably when executing their statutory public interest duties; (2) courts must reevaluate the understanding of what constitutes ratably decision-making in utility regulation; (3) courts should ask, “Is decision-making that marginalize environmental impacts ratably?”
utility regulators should integrate environmental impacts into their “public interest’ analysis.
utility regulators should integrate environmental considerations into “public interest,” and courts should demand it.
In summary, our research is concerned with
how courts can and should evaluate regulators’ treatment of environmental impacts.
how regulators and courts can best interpret “public interest” obligations to ensure rational decision-making in electricity regulation.
the question of when regulators may disregard environmental impacts in executing their “ public interest” duties.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
regulators must take the environment into account when making “public interest” decisions.
the environment should be considered when the “public interest” demands it.
regulators can ignore the environment only when they can demonstrate that the environment is not a material consideration in the relevant statutory “public interest.”
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the environment is not always a material consideration in utility regulation.
utility regulators should consider environmental impacts whenever those impacts are material to their “public interest duties,” but not when they are not.
regulators must take environmental impacts into account when executing their statutory public interest duties, but that the environment does not necessarily have to be a primary consideration.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the “public interest” doctrine is not an environmental trump card.
utility regulators can only make sensible decisions if they integrate environmental analysis into “cost-minimization, nondiscriminatory access, and service adequacy.”
the environment is often relevant to “public interest” decision-making – even if it is not always the most relevant issue.
